title: Waves and sound
blurb: Describe transverse and longitudinal waves, use v = fλ and f = 1/T, and explain sound speed, pitch, loudness, decibels, echoes, ultrasound and the Doppler effect.
question: A sonographer's ultrasound pulse returns from an organ a fraction of a millisecond after it is sent. How do you find the organ's depth, why can't we hear the pulse, and why does a passing siren change pitch?

teach.body: Formally, a wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from place to place without transferring matter. In plain English: the medium wiggles in place while the energy travels on. Mechanical waves (sound, water waves, a wave on a rope) need a medium. Electromagnetic waves, such as light, do not: they cross the vacuum of space. That is why there is light, but no sound, between Earth and the Sun.

Amplitude is the maximum displacement from rest and sets the energy (loudness of sound, brightness of light). Wavelength (λ) is the distance from one crest or compression to the next, in meters. Frequency (f) is waves per second, in hertz; period T = 1/f. Wave speed v = fλ. The medium sets the speed, so in one medium a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength, and the speed does not change.

items: Wavelength: sound at 680 Hz in air (v = 340 m/s). λ = v ÷ f = 340 ÷ 680 = 0.50 m.
Speed: λ = 2.0 m and T = 0.50 s, so f = 2.0 Hz and v = 2.0 × 2.0 = 4.0 m/s.
Echo: a shout returns after 1.0 s (v = 340 m/s). Round trip 340 m, so the wall is 170 m away.
Same medium, frequency doubled: wavelength halves, speed unchanged.

teach.body: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave. It travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases, and not at all in a vacuum; in air it is roughly 340 m/s (the stem gives the value). Pitch depends on frequency; loudness on amplitude, measured in decibels: each +10 dB is 10 times the intensity. Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Ultrasound lies above that range (sonography); infrasound lies below it.

teach.caption: +20 dB is 10 × 10 = 100 times the intensity, not 2 or 20 times.

head: Behavior
What happens
Example
teach.caption: Doppler: a source moving toward you sounds higher, moving away lower. Resonance: driving an object at its natural frequency builds a large amplitude.

teach.body: Nia, a diagnostic medical sonography applicant, sends an ultrasound pulse into soft tissue, where it travels at 1,500 m/s (given). The echo returns 0.000080 s later. The round trip is 1,500 × 0.000080 = 0.12 m, so the boundary is half that: 0.060 m, or 6.0 cm deep. The pulse is above 20,000 Hz, so nobody hears it. A Doppler setting uses the frequency shift of echoes from moving blood to measure flow.

teach.text: Sound is longitudinal, needs a medium and is fastest in solids, slowest in air. Waves carry energy, not matter. Pitch is frequency; loudness is amplitude. Changing frequency in the same medium changes wavelength, not speed. Approaching sources sound higher. Halve the echo distance. +20 dB is 100 times the intensity.

items: Waves transfer energy, not matter; sound needs a medium, light does not.
v = fλ and T = 1/f; the medium sets the speed.
Sound: fastest in solids; pitch = frequency; loudness = amplitude; +10 dB = 10 × intensity.
Echo distance = speed × time ÷ 2; Doppler: approaching = higher pitch.

summary: You can now tell transverse from longitudinal waves, link amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period, and use v = fλ. You can also explain how sound travels, what sets pitch and loudness, how decibels scale, how echoes and ultrasound measure distance and how the Doppler effect shifts pitch.

A.q: Which of these waves can travel through a vacuum?
A.why: Light is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium, so it crosses a vacuum.

whyNot.0: Sound is a mechanical wave; it needs particles to vibrate.
whyNot.2: A water wave needs water: it is a mechanical wave.
whyNot.3: A rope wave needs the rope: it is a mechanical wave.

A.q: Which property of a sound wave determines its pitch?
A.why: Pitch is how high or low a sound is, and it depends on frequency.

whyNot.1: In one medium, all sounds travel at about the same speed whatever their pitch.
whyNot.2: Intensity is the energy flow that sets loudness, measured in decibels.

A.q: A wave has a frequency of 5.0 Hz. What is its period?

whyNot.1: 5.0 is the frequency in hertz, not the period.

B.q: A wave on a rope has a frequency of 4.0 Hz and a wavelength of 1.5 m. What is its speed?

whyNot.3: Adds the two values instead of multiplying.

B.q: Thunder is heard 3.0 s after the lightning flash is seen. Using 340 m/s for the speed of sound, about how far away is the storm?
B.why: The light arrives almost instantly; the sound travels one way: 340 × 3.0 = 1,020 m.

whyNot.0: Halves the distance as for an echo; thunder travels one way only.
whyNot.2: Divides speed by time instead of multiplying.
whyNot.3: Doubles the distance as if the sound made a round trip.

B.q: In which of these does sound travel the slowest?
B.why: Sound is slowest in gases, faster in liquids and fastest in solids. Air is the only gas listed.

whyNot.0: Water is a liquid; sound travels faster in it than in air.
whyNot.1: Steel is a solid, where sound travels fastest.
whyNot.3: Glass is a solid; sound travels faster in it than in air.

C.q: An ultrasound pulse travels through soft tissue at 1,500 m/s and its echo returns from a boundary 0.00010 s after it is sent. How deep is the boundary?

whyNot.0: 15 cm is the round trip; halve it for the depth.
whyNot.1: Slips a decimal place when converting 0.075 m to centimeters.
whyNot.2: Halves twice; the round trip is halved once.

C.q: A sound rises from 40 dB to 70 dB. By what factor does its intensity increase?
C.why: +30 dB is three steps of +10 dB, each × 10: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000.

whyNot.1: Treats decibels as a linear scale; each 10 dB step multiplies intensity by 10.
whyNot.2: Counts four tenfold steps; 70 − 40 = 30 dB is three steps.
whyNot.3: Multiplies 3 steps by 100; three tenfold steps give 1,000.

C.q: A guitarist shortens a string so its note rises in frequency, while the wave speed on the string stays the same. What happens to the wavelength?
C.why: v = fλ with v fixed: a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.

whyNot.0: Wavelength and frequency are inversely related at a fixed speed.
whyNot.2: With speed fixed, a change in frequency must change the wavelength.
whyNot.3: Amplitude does not enter v = fλ.

reteach.title: The stadium wave
reteach.question: When a crowd does 'the wave' around a stadium, what actually travels around the stands?

blocks.h: The pattern moves, the people do not
blocks.body: Each fan stands up and sits down in place, yet a ripple races around the stadium. The fans are the medium; the ripple is the wave; the stand-and-sit is its energy passing along. Nobody ends up in another seat: waves carry energy, not matter. Fans moving up and down while the wave moves sideways is a transverse wave. If instead each fan nudged the next one sideways along the row, the wave would be longitudinal, like sound.

blocks.text: Take the fans away and the wave cannot exist. Take the air away and sound cannot travel: that is why space is silent.

explain.h: Which way do the particles move?
explain.body: Perpendicular to the wave's travel: transverse. Parallel to it: longitudinal.

test.q: A spring toy is pushed so its coils move back and forth along the toy's length as the wave travels. What type of wave is this?
test.why: The coils move parallel to the direction the wave travels: a longitudinal wave, like sound.

whyNot.0: Transverse waves move the medium perpendicular to the travel direction.
whyNot.2: Electromagnetic waves need no medium; this wave travels through the coils.
whyNot.3: Surface waves, like ripples on water, move particles in circles, not along the length.

explain.body: f = v ÷ λ and λ = v ÷ f. Divide the speed by the quantity you know.

test.q: A sound traveling at 340 m/s has a wavelength of 0.85 m. What is its frequency?

explain.body: Pitch follows frequency. Loudness follows amplitude. Change one without the other.

test.q: Which change makes a sound louder without changing its pitch?
test.why: Loudness depends on amplitude; keeping the frequency fixed keeps the pitch the same.

whyNot.0: A higher frequency raises the pitch.
whyNot.1: A shorter wavelength in the same medium means a higher frequency, so a higher pitch.
whyNot.3: A lower frequency lowers the pitch.

explain.body: Source approaching: waves bunch up, higher frequency and pitch. Source moving away: waves spread out, lower pitch.

test.q: A train sounding its horn moves away from you. Compared with the horn's true pitch, the pitch you hear is:
test.why: A source moving away is heard at a lower frequency, so a lower pitch (Doppler effect).

whyNot.0: A higher pitch is heard while the source approaches.
whyNot.1: Motion of the source shifts the frequency you hear.
whyNot.2: A receding horn grows softer, and its pitch drops too.
